## About the package

`cdogmar` replicates the central dogma of molecular biology: DNA is transcribed into RNA, and RNA is translated into protein. The package contains five small functions, one for each step, and a standard codon table (`codon_table`) that maps the 64 RNA codons to single-letter amino acid codes (stop codons are `_`).

```{r setup}
library(cdogmar)
```

## The functions one by one

`generate_dna()` creates a random DNA sequence of a given length. We set a seed so the example is reproducible.

```{r}
set.seed(42)
dna <- generate_dna(sequence_length = 30)
dna
```

`transcribe_dna()` transcribes DNA into RNA by replacing every thymine (T) with uracil (U).

```{r}
rna <- transcribe_dna(dna)
rna
```

`split_codons()` splits a sequence into codons of three nucleotides. The `start` argument sets the reading frame, and an incomplete last codon is dropped.

```{r}
codons <- split_codons(rna, start = 1)
codons
```

`codons_to_amino_acids()` translates the codons into a protein sequence using `codon_table`.

```{r}
protein <- codons_to_amino_acids(codons)
protein
```

`plot_amino_acid_counts()` counts how often each amino acid occurs and returns a ggplot bar chart.

```{r}
plot_amino_acid_counts(protein)
```

## All functions together

Because each function's output is the next function's input, the whole central dogma can be written as one pipeline:

```{r}
set.seed(42)
generate_dna(sequence_length = 300) |>
  transcribe_dna() |>
  split_codons() |>
  codons_to_amino_acids() |>
  plot_amino_acid_counts()
```

## Use cases and possible extensions

`cdogmar` is mainly a teaching tool: it shows each step of gene expression in a few lines of code, and the random sequences make it easy to explore how codon usage shapes amino acid frequencies. Useful extra functions could be: finding the start codon (AUG) and translating only the open reading frame up to the first stop codon, making the reverse complement of a DNA strand, calculating GC content, translating all three reading frames and reading real sequences from FASTA files.

## Group discussion

**Dependencies.** `plot_amino_acid_counts()` needs `ggplot2` for plotting and `stringr` for splitting and counting characters. They are added as dependencies by listing them under `Imports` in the `DESCRIPTION` file (which is what `usethis::use_package()` does), so they are installed together with `cdogmar`.

**Why limit dependencies?** Every dependency must be installed by the user, makes installation slower, and can break our package if it changes or is removed. Dependencies cannot always be avoided: rewriting a plotting system like `ggplot2` ourselves would be much more work and much more error-prone than relying on a well-tested package.

**`@importFrom` vs `package::function()`.** An `@importFrom stringr str_count` tag adds the function to the package's `NAMESPACE`, so it can be called as `str_count()` without a prefix. Writing `stringr::str_count()` instead shows exactly where each function comes from and avoids name clashes. In both cases the package must still be listed under `Imports`.
